The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged at its latest meeting, but the signal from Chair Kevin Warsh was enough to rattle markets. Warsh indicated that rate hikes are back on the table if inflation does not continue to ease, a hawkish pivot that caught Wall Street off guard, according to the New York Post.

The FOMC statement flagged inflation as the committee's primary concern, and Warsh's tone in the press conference reinforced that framing. Futures markets, which had been pricing in at least one cut before year-end, shifted quickly - traders are now assigning meaningful probability to a hike scenario.

The move marks a notable departure from the dovish drift that had dominated Fed communication in recent months. Whether this is a genuine recalibration or a warning shot to keep inflation expectations anchored is the question markets will be working through for the next several weeks.

The deal that gives Iran everything — and asks for nothing 

The preliminary U.S.-Iran agreement hands Tehran a stunning economic windfall while demanding almost nothing in return.

Iran gets immediate oil export waivers worth billions, the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade, and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz — all without having to actually dismantle its nuclear program. And the hardest concessions Washington claimed it wanted got postponed to a 60-day negotiation window that experts say is far too short to resolve decades of nuclear tension. 

Iran resumes oil exports that were worth an estimated $46 billion in 2024, receives the unfreezing of around $24 billion in frozen assets, and is promised a jaw-dropping $300 billion reconstruction fund. In exchange? A vague commitment to "downblend" some highly enriched uranium under IAEA supervision — with all the technical details left for later. Iran's missile program, its proxy network in Lebanon, and even the fate of its theocratic government — original U.S. war aims — aren't even on the negotiating table.

Tehran's own media is selling the deal as outright victory — "the political codification of a battlefield reality". Even expert Nicole Grajewski of Sciences Po concludes: "Judged solely on the memorandum itself, the immediate and concrete benefits accrue disproportionately to Iran."

Trump called the 2015 nuclear deal the "worst deal ever." This one makes that look like a masterstroke of diplomacy.
